title: Jeppesen ForeFlight's First Airflow Agents Are an OCC Story — and That's More Revealing Than It Looks
summary: The premier EFB and cockpit-software brand just launched its first agentic AI tools aimed squarely at crew scheduling and disruption management, not the flightdeck — and the sequencing choice tells us something concrete about where aviation AI finds its first commercial footholds.
body_markdown:
I've written before about how the aviation industry keeps treating cockpit AI as a liability problem while continuing to invest freely on the operations side. Jeppesen ForeFlight's Airflow agent debut on October 6 — the first real product output from the agentic AI strategy the company introduced in July — gives that argument a fresh and unusually pointed illustration.

## What Was Actually Launched

<cite index="25-1,25-2">Jeppesen ForeFlight unveiled the first of hundreds of planned agents for its Airflow Aviation Operating Intelligence platform, with customers able to bring or build their own agents, use Jeppesen ForeFlight's, third-party tools, or combine them.</cite> <cite index="22-7,22-8,22-9,22-10,22-11">The three initial agents cover trip trading — helping crews exchange trips more quickly and fairly — target mastery, intended to eliminate trial and error in pairing and roster planning by translating planners' targets around cost, fatigue, and robustness into a workable plan — and augmented ops control, which helps operators manage disruptions by evaluating and ranking all recovery options with reasoning attached.</cite>

<cite index="25-3">All agents run on an aviation-centric context layer, with customer data remaining sovereign, governance grounded in the industry's Safety Management System framework, and configurable automation levels that keep humans at the center of decisions.</cite> <cite index="25-5">Every recommendation carries the facts, sources, and reasoning behind it, so operators can review a decision rather than take it on faith.</cite> That traceability architecture is the right call for aviation, and Jeppesen ForeFlight deserves credit for building it in from the start rather than bolting it on later.

<cite index="22-5">The rollout advances one of Jeppesen's first new major ventures since Boeing sold it and ForeFlight to private equity firm Thoma Bravo in April 2025.</cite> <cite index="27-7,27-8">Additional agents for business and military aviation segments will also debut soon, and the company has already begun seeking commercial aviation partners for its co-development phase ahead of a broader rollout early next year.</cite>

## The Sequencing Question

Here's the opinion: the company that built its reputation on charts, EFBs, and pilot-facing navigation tools just launched its first AI agents aimed primarily at crew scheduling and the OCC. <cite index="20-9">The first tools are aimed primarily at crew scheduling and operational disruptions rather than functions used directly by pilots.</cite> That's not a criticism — it's a strategy, and it's probably the right one.

Crew scheduling and disruption recovery are genuinely solvable problems for agentic AI right now. The data is structured, the rules are codified (fatigue regulations, collective agreements, reserve policies), and the cost of a wrong recommendation is measurable and recoverable — a planner can override a bad trip-trade suggestion in seconds. That's a fundamentally different risk profile from putting an AI agent in front of a flight crew mid-flight, where the window for human review narrows considerably and the consequences of a bad output are orders of magnitude higher.

Having spent years on the delivery side of aviation software, I've watched vendors repeatedly underestimate how much trust accumulation an airline requires before it hands a new system any real authority over an operational decision. The OCC is where that trust gets built — through audit logs, override rates, and eventually a track record. What Jeppesen ForeFlight is doing with Airflow isn't retreating from the cockpit; it's building the institutional credibility that eventually earns it a seat there.

## What This Means for the Cockpit Path

The deeper implication is architectural. <cite index="22-3,22-4">Jeppesen unveiled three AI agents as the first of hundreds it plans to introduce on the platform, and the company contrasted generic AI systems — which it said sound confident but are often wrong — with what it bills as more trustworthy "aviation intelligence" that uses a working model of the ecosystem the agent is analyzing.</cite> That "working model of the ecosystem" framing is the important part. If Airflow's context layer is genuinely built to reason about operational cause and effect across crew, fleet, and flight data simultaneously, then the jump from OCC agents to cockpit-adjacent agents — think flight planning input, fuel advisory, weather routing — is an architectural extension, not a rebuild.

That's the bet worth watching. Right now Airflow is an OCC play. Whether the aviation-centric reasoning layer it's building today actually extends cleanly to pilot-facing use cases is the question that will define whether this platform becomes something genuinely new, or simply a more sophisticated version of what the crew management vendors have been selling for two decades.

I covered Jeppesen ForeFlight's earlier AI feature push back in July, when ClearNOTAMs and the ChatGPT connector were the headliners. The Airflow agents debut is a different kind of announcement — not a feature, but a platform commitment, with a roadmap that implies scale. Whether the roadmap survives contact with airline procurement cycles is the next test.

questions: The first Airflow agents target crew scheduling and disruption management — not the cockpit. Does that sequencing surprise you, or does it strike you as the strategically correct starting point? (Surprising / Correct move / Mixed)

From your time on the delivery and product side of aviation software, how long does it typically take a new AI platform to build enough of an operational track record in the OCC before an airline would even consider piloting it in a cockpit-adjacent workflow — months, or years?

Jeppesen ForeFlight describes Airflow as reasoning through 'operational cause and effect rather than general pattern matching.' In your read, is that a meaningful architectural distinction from what other vendors are calling agentic AI — or is it mostly marketing language at this stage?

The platform is designed so customers can bring or build their own agents, not just consume Jeppesen ForeFlight's. Does that open-platform posture change how you'd evaluate Airflow against a more closed, vertically-integrated alternative — and is an airline actually equipped to build its own agents on top of it?

Given that Jeppesen ForeFlight's core brand equity is in the cockpit and on the EFB side, is there a risk that leading with OCC agents dilutes that positioning — or is the 'platform for all of flight ops' framing actually stronger than either cockpit-only or OCC-only?
email_brief: On October 6, 2026, Jeppesen ForeFlight unveiled the first agents for its Airflow 'Aviation Operating Intelligence' platform — the agentic AI strategy the company introduced in July after being sold by Boeing to Thoma Bravo in April 2025. The three initial agents cover crew trip trading, schedule/pairing optimization, and disruption recovery in the OCC. Notably, none of the first agents are pilot-facing or cockpit-adjacent, even though ForeFlight built its brand as the premier EFB and cockpit-software platform. Today's post is framed as an opinion piece arguing that this OCC-first sequencing is actually the strategically correct move — and that the more interesting question is whether the aviation-centric reasoning layer being built for the OCC can extend cleanly to cockpit-adjacent use cases later. This is relevant right now because it illustrates a broader pattern in aviation AI: structured, recoverable, high-data-density OCC problems are getting solved first, while pilot-facing AI keeps being deferred.
